task: Write one sentence of your own using the word puerile. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know puerile should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Forty years on, the twins' puerile ritual survives: whoever says 'jinx' first owns the other's dessert.
Silly is milder than puerile — light foolishness that nobody needs to outgrow.
Infantile is harsher than puerile: puerile conduct belongs on a playground, while infantile conduct belongs in a crib.

Childish means acting like a child, and anyone can say it — warmly of a game, sharply of a coworker. Puerile is the critic's colder version: it always passes judgment, scolding grown people for conduct beneath their age. A birthday party can be happily childish; only a fault is puerile.

Sophomoric mocks immaturity that thinks itself clever — the smug dorm-room philosopher, jokes proud of their own daring. Puerile is the plainer judgment: conduct or humor that is simply juvenile, with no pretension of sophistication required. Sophomoric faults the self-satisfaction; puerile faults the immaturity itself.

Latin puer, 'boy,' fathered almost nothing else in common English — puerility is just this word's own noun, and the rest of the family stayed behind in Latin. Puerile stands alone, fittingly for a word about refusing to grow.
Puerile means juvenile, immature.
The film critic spent four paragraphs dismissing the blockbuster's humor as puerile — food fights, rude noises, a fart joke with a sequel — and one closing sentence confessing he had laughed twice.
Puerile is a judgment, not a description of age: it scolds grown people for humor or conduct that belongs in a school corridor.
A child's silliness is just childish; it earns puerile only when someone old enough to know better keeps it up.
Puerile is the critic's word for immaturity — cooler and more cutting than childish, which anyone might say warmly of a game.
Its unit neighbor petulance names one specific immature display, the sulk; puerile passes judgment on the whole performance.
Save infantile for when you want the insult absolute.
